text:
Chapter Six


At some point, the relentless mist had dissipated, leaving only low, drifting gray clouds, so Maggie parked her car a few blocks away from Rodrigo’s. As she spun the wheel to slide into a tight spot, the Beltane mask swung from her rearview mirror, and she felt a not-unpleasant blush creep across her cheeks as she thought again of how she’d opened up for the stranger.


Last night, as she’d tossed and turned, she’d tried again to unravel the magic of the mask, excavating her memories for anything that might help. But instead of anything concrete about him, she just recalled again the way desire had coiled hot in her belly while his hands had traced the soft swells of her shoulders, breasts, hips, as if he had been trying to memorize every inch of her. And then there’d been the way he’d kissed, the way he’d done everything that night, with a kind of shy confidence. It had been so charming. So different from the way Taliesin reminded everyone of how brilliant he was at every turn.


In downtown Galloway, the faefire glow of the streetlamps reflected off the still-damp road in shining halos of light. Galloway was, technically, a small coastal hamlet, but between here and the beach was ten miles of uninhabited, near impassable Wilds. Part forest and part swamp, the Wilds were a strange, overgrown place full of tangled brambles and creatures touched by myth and magic. The edge of the Wilds crept up behind Ilex Hall, and it had unsettled Maggie since her first trip to campus for her interview four and a half years ago. But because travelers had to go nearly twenty miles around the Wilds to get to the ocean, Galloway didn’t get the same amount of tourist traffic as other coastal towns did. That meant that most of the people walking the streets were students or people who lived in Galloway year-round.


Galloway and Hawthorn were never quite what she had envisioned for herself and her career. But her entire life had gone up in smoke during graduate school, all thanks to her ex, Evan. The scars of that time still stretched her skin. Personal and professional relationships soured; a promising career opportunity disappeared into dust. She’d had to start over on the other side of the country, alone.


Good had come out of it, too. She and Dahlia had started as professors at Hawthorn the same year, Maggie in the Applied Linguistics and Incantation Translation Department and Dahlia in Runology and Sigil Studies. Their friendship was forged in the fire of trying to figure out how to balance teaching and research and the endless politics of academia. She had come to love Hawthorn and Galloway, too. A small college in a small town, with a close-knit community of colleagues and friends she wouldn’t dream of risking. Not again.


Maggie’s heart felt full and grateful as she looked around at the town that had become her home while she waited for Dahlia to get out of the car. “Rodrigo saved us two good seats at the bar,” Dahlia said as she shut the door. “We’ll be able to keep an eye on the crowd for a mysterious, six-foot-one man with a little brother.”


“I’m never telling you anything ever again,” Maggie grumbled.


“Now that is a lie.”


“He’s not going to be in Galloway. Brig Beach and Atlantia are miles away,” Maggie reasoned.


“Then you have nothing to be nervous about, do you?”


“Who says I’m nervous?” Dahlia looked down her nose at her. “Fine, I’m nervous. What if he’s married?”


“What if he’s not?” Dahlia reasoned.


“What if he’s an asshole? I have enough of those to deal with during the day.”


“No one is as big an asshole as Arthur Taliesin. C’mon.”



—


Rodrigo’s drinks were strong and dangerously delicious, which helped because Maggie felt a little silly, sitting on a stool in the corner of the bar, watching the crowd for anyone who might trigger some sort of memory. Chasing a man around town? What am I, an undergrad? She recognized probably a third of the people in Rodrigo’s that night, but none of the strangers fit the thin description she had of the man from Beltane.


Rodrigo’s was, affectionately, a dive. The building was ancient, with low ceilings and old stained-glass lamps. On one side of the room was a sweeping bar, polished to gleaming, and on the other were low, overstuffed couches and booths. Upstairs, there were fraying pool tables, dartboards, and groups playing card games or mahjong. Dahlia had already been up there to scope out the people playing games and sipping on beer but returned with nothing much to report. “It’s the same crowd as always.”


“Oh, that’s too bad,” Maggie said, but she had a small grin on her face, and her voice was cheerful. She could enjoy the night with Dahlia, chat with Rodrigo while he was in between customers, and be spectacularly annoyed about Arthur Taliesin. She knew that Dahlia just wanted to see her happy. She knew that because if the situation were reversed, she would turn over heaven and earth to find a masked stranger for Dahlia.


“Who are you looking for?” asked Rodrigo, the burly owner of his eponymous bar.


“Maggie’s in love,” Dahlia interjected before Maggie could explain.


Rodrigo grinned as he mixed a drink. “Who’s the lucky person?”


“Would you stop telling people I’m in love? We’ve got to work on boundaries, Dahlia.” Maggie sighed. “I met someone at the Beltane festival on Brig Beach, but I don’t know his name.”


A playful smirk turned up the corners of Rodrigo’s mouth. “We’ve all been there, haven’t we? What does he look like?”


“Well,” she said, dragging out the sound, “I don’t really know that either.” She explained the masks, and the way he’d charmed her, and that she didn’t know how she’d let Dahlia talk her into trying to find him. “Your bar is on every Best Of list this side of Atlantia. We figured there’s as good a chance as any that he’d come through here one day.”


“What do you know about him?”


Dahlia reached into her sweater pocket and pulled out a sticky note. It matched the list Maggie had erased from her chalkboard, but Dahlia had added two more details she had coaxed out of Maggie. Calls himself TK. Thirty-five. She passed it over to Rodrigo.


He took it, holding it up to the light and an arm’s length away because he wasn’t wearing his reading glasses. “This is it? At least six one?”


Dahlia gave Rodrigo an appraising look. “You’re tall,” she said, as if it was the first time she noticed. “Maggie, if you stood next to Rodrigo, do you think you’d remember how tall TK was?”


Maggie shrugged, unsure whether the mask’s magic would let her hold on to that much detail, but she hopped off her stool and ducked under the bar door. Rodrigo threw his towel over his shoulder and opened his arms, inviting Maggie in for a hug.


She and Dahlia had known Rodrigo for almost as long as they’d known each other, after they met him during an event he’d catered for Hawthorn. She didn’t mind that he knew about the mystery man; she probably would have told him herself later in the evening when she was two drinks in and cared less about keeping her own secrets.


“She’s lucky she’s funny,” Maggie said into Rodrigo’s bicep. “I can’t believe we put up with her.” Rodrigo chuckled, the sound resonating through his chest, and Maggie could admit that, maybe, she needed this hug. His arms wrapped around her, pulling her close in a crushing embrace, and Maggie eased into it, sighing. She thought, as she often did when she spent time with Rodrigo, that this must be what it felt like to have an older brother.


The top of Maggie’s head barely reached Rodrigo’s shoulder, and she estimated that her mysterious stranger was probably an inch taller than her friend. She gave him a squeeze, and he let her go. “How tall are you, Ro?” Dahlia asked.


“I’m six one,” Rodrigo said. “Making him…”


“I came up to here on him,” Maggie confirmed, playing along for both of them. She gestured to a spot about an inch below where her head had rested at Rodrigo’s collarbone.


“I’d say he’s probably six two, then,” Rodrigo said, and Dahlia grabbed the list from the bar where Rodrigo had left it, made the update, and handed it back to him.


“Put this behind the bar, and if you see anyone who matches this description, call me immediately.”


Rodrigo’s eyebrows rose as he took the list, but then he stuck it next to the blender and said, “For you and you alone, Dahlia.”


As Maggie returned to her stool, she felt that familiar embarrassment creeping up her ears, red and hot. “Can we talk about something else now?” she asked Dahlia. Rodrigo wandered back to the other end of the bar, cleaning glasses and taking a drink order from another customer.


Her friend looked at her thoughtfully. “You know, if you want me to stop trying to find him, I’ll stop.”


Maggie bit her lip. Was that what she wanted? She realized very quickly that the answer was no. She couldn’t quite let go of TK, not with how he’d kissed her, how neatly their bodies had fit together as they danced to the music on Beltane. If she had the chance…she’d really like to kiss him again. At least one more time. “No,” Maggie finally replied. “I want to keep looking. I’ve just been so distracted. One more thing Taliesin and his pall are ruining.”


Rodrigo had returned, setting sweating glasses of water on coasters in front of them. “Arthur Taliesin?” When Maggie nodded, Rodrigo went on. “I heard he was teaching up at the school. I keep meaning to get to one of his community lectures, but I haven’t had the time.”


“You’re not missing much,” Maggie muttered with that grumpy, petulant edge she couldn’t seem to shake whenever she talked about Taliesin. It wasn’t even a true statement. Maggie had been to one of his community lectures, and it was great. Dahlia looked at her pointedly. “Ugh, fine. He is a genius. If you get a chance, you really should go to one of them.”


“But?” Rodrigo asked.


“He’s annoying!” Maggie practically shouted. “I don’t care if he’s brilliant. He’s a legacy academic who has never worked a real job a day in his life.”


Maggie had gone to school with plenty of people like Taliesin. People for whom a career in academia was a foregone conclusion. People whose parents and grandparents were academics or who carried the same name as a building on campus, usually because they had more ambition than brain cells and their families had more money than sense.


Her own academic trajectory was so different that she could hardly relate to most of her classmates who came from that world. A love of Diadhan had steered her toward academia. She had been so sure that it was what she wanted—the imagined prestige and influence—that she had worked with a singular focus to get the best spot she could in the best possible program. It had been grueling, nearly crushing the love she had for the Diadhan language. Even now, she wasn’t always sure it was worth it. She had been competing with people who understood the language and culture of academia in a way she hadn’t. People like Taliesin, who had known from the time they were kids that professor was a job people could have.


Maggie’s parents had always been very practical. Her father owned a small greenspell business and her mother worked the desk, answering phones and scheduling appointments. To Maggie, it seemed they saw their only daughter as something strange and not wholly theirs. She knew they loved her, but, to them, she had little to show for all the stress she went through in undergrad and grad school. They didn’t quite understand what she had worked so hard for all those years. There had been times when Maggie hadn’t either.


Dahlia took another sip of her drink, hiding a bemused-but-critical look behind the glass. “What?” Maggie asked, eyes narrowed.


“I’m not sure that’s totally fair,” Dahlia said carefully, and Maggie’s cheeks reddened, burning hotter because of the alcohol.


“Well, whatever happened last week with the pall was absolutely his fault, but he won’t admit it.”


Rodrigo’s eyes grew wide. “That explains it. I’ve had to call the wardsmiths to replace our basement wards twice since Beltane. At least one ghoul got in there and made a huge mess of a sack of sugar.”


The banshee screeches at night were bad enough, but Maggie was glad she didn’t have any ghouls scratching at her windows. She made a mental note to strengthen the lone ward she kept active on her front door. “When did they dissipate the pall?” Rodrigo asked.


Dahlia leaned in and said quietly, “It’s still there.”


“Since Beltane?!” He let out a low whistle. “Yikes.”


“It’s taken over the entire third floor of our building. We’re sharing offices and classrooms to try to make up for the lost space,” Maggie explained.


“And Maggie won the lottery and is sharing her office with the Arthur Taliesin.”


“More like got the short stick,” Maggie grumbled, her burning cheeks forgotten as she ticked off her fingers and went down a long list of complaints. “He refuses to come up with a reasonable schedule for sharing our office. He thinks his own program is more important than mine. He can’t sit still. He judges the way I teach…”


Dahlia held out a hand, interrupting Maggie. “I need you to elaborate on that last one. What could he possibly have to judge about the way you teach?”


“He overheard one of my phonology students ask for an extension on her paper, and, of course, he told me I was getting taken advantage of.” Dahlia rolled her eyes so dramatically that Rodrigo laughed, and Maggie was thrilled to have Dahlia back on her side. “You should have heard him.” Maggie furrowed her eyebrows and lowered her voice an octave. “Our jobs are to prepare them for the real world.”


Before Maggie realized it, Rodrigo had set another drink in front of her and she was sipping on it happily, complaining about Taliesin and blowing off steam. And when the drink was half-gone and she felt buzzy and fuzzy, she said out loud, “And he just smells too good. It’s not fair.” Her eyes went wide as she looked to see if Dahlia had heard what she said, and, sure enough, her friend’s mouth dropped open in shock.


“Oh, no, ignore that,” Maggie pleaded.


“I will not. He smells good? Why are you so close you’re smelling him?”


“It’s a ten-by-ten room, of course I can smell him,” Maggie reasoned. “Like you haven’t noticed how attractive he is.”


“Well, sure, I have. I just didn’t know you had. All I’ve heard about is how miserable he is.”


“You can be miserable and hot,” Maggie said, frowning into her cup.


Dahlia tipped her glass toward Maggie’s, and they clinked them together. “I’ll drink to that.”

facts.fact: 她与 Dahlia 同年入职（应用语言学/符文印符系），友谊在学界政治的火里锻造。
便利贴添 TK/35 两条递给 Rodrigo；六尺一的 Rodrigo 拥抱校准出神秘人约六尺二。
Dahlia 提出可停手；她想到吻与严丝合缝的共舞，答继续找。
阶级自白：父亲 greenspell 小店/母亲看柜台——独生女不完全是他们的。
Rodrigo 听说 pall：地窖结界两周修两次、ghoul 闹翻糖袋。
半杯酒后说漏嘴他就是太好闻了；碰杯定格又惨又 hot 可以并存。
facts.anchor: You can be miserable and hot
